title: Skyrocketing School Fees Are Squeezing Indian Families as Education Inflation Outpaces Income Growth
excerpt: With private school costs rising 10 to 12 percent annually and coaching expenses nearly matching tuition by secondary school, Indian families are caught between aspiration and affordability.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Education inflation in India is 10-12% annually, significantly outpacing income growth.
  • Total schooling costs in Mumbai range from ₹7.9 lakh to ₹61.2 lakh from nursery to Class XII.
  • Nearly 40% of secondary students enroll in private coaching, with costs nearly matching school fees.
  • Hidden costs like transport and extracurriculars often exceed base tuition, surprising families annually.

  • Education inflation in India runs at 10 to 12 percent annually, roughly double the headline consumer price index, with some schools hiking fees by as much as 42 percent in a single year.
  • The total cost of schooling a child from nursery to Class XII in Mumbai ranges from ₹7.9 lakh at affordable private schools to ₹61.2 lakh at elite institutions, according to a 2026 report by 1 Finance.
  • By secondary school, nearly two in five Indian students are enrolled in private coaching, and tuition spending on coaching almost equals formal school fees.
  • Hidden costs — transport, technology, uniforms, and extracurricular activities — routinely match or exceed base tuition, catching families off guard year after year.

A nursery seat in Mumbai now costs more per year than an entire four-year engineering degree at IIT Bombay did a decade ago. That comparison, made viral by investor Aviral Bhatnagar on X, captures a financial reality that millions of Indian families are living through: the cost of educating a child is rising faster than almost anything else in the household budget.

The Numbers Behind the Squeeze

The 1 Finance Global Economic Outlook 2026 Report quantifies the damage. In Mumbai alone, educating a child from nursery through Class XII costs between ₹7.9 lakh at an affordable private school and ₹61.2 lakh at an elite one. Education inflation runs at 10 to 12 percent annually — roughly double the official consumer price index of 5 to 6 percent — and some schools have pushed through increases as high as 42 percent in a single year, according to the report.

The gap between what families budget and what they actually pay widens every year, eating into retirement savings, emergency funds, or adding to household debt.

"India's middle class has always treated education as the one expense you don't question. That instinct is being exploited. Schools raise fees 10 to 12 percent a year because they know parents won't pull their children out in Class VI over a fee hike."

— Animesh Hardia, SVP, Quantitative Research, 1 Finance

The Shadow Education System

Formal school fees tell only part of the story. A Comprehensive Modular Survey on Education conducted across more than 52,000 households in 2025 found that nearly two in five secondary school students — up from under a quarter in primary school — are enrolled in private coaching classes. By the time students reach senior secondary level, coaching expenditure claims nearly 47 percent of total education spending, almost matching formal school fees, according to analysis by the Centre for Economic Data and Analysis at Ashoka University.

Average coaching costs rise from ₹525 at the pre-primary level to ₹6,311 at higher secondary. Urban families bear the brunt: spending in cities is nearly three times rural levels through middle school.

Senior educationist Kishore Darak, who has worked in the sector for close to three decades, described coaching as a structural dependency. "Entry to higher education is now almost totally driven by entrance examinations and the coaching industry is the gatekeeper there," he told IndiaSpend. "Coaching centres teach techniques of cracking exams. Almost any child cannot crack those exams without such coaching support."

Beyond tuition and coaching, families face a web of ancillary expenses that are rarely regulated or even transparently disclosed. Transport can run between ₹40,000 and ₹1.5 lakh per year. Co-curricular activities add ₹50,000 to ₹3 lakh. Technology kits, uniforms, books, and development charges — often framed as one-time fees but charged annually — pile on further.

An average student in a private school incurs ₹28,693 per year in education-related costs, roughly 10 times the ₹2,863 spent per student in government schools, the 2025 survey found. For many well-earning families, the total annual per-child outlay can consume 40 to 80 percent of household income.

What This Means for NRI Families

The cost squeeze reaches Indian families regardless of geography. Parents in the diaspora who send children to schools in India face the same 10 to 12 percent annual fee escalation. Those educating children abroad encounter even steeper costs: studying overseas runs between ₹30 lakh and ₹1 crore or more, according to a Kotak Mutual Fund report. Indian families spent $3.7 billion on overseas education in 2025 alone.

Digital coaching platforms have extended the shadow education system across borders, meaning NRI families often pay for private tutoring on top of already expensive international school fees.

Darak argues the solution must be structural. "If India wants to become a developed country, it should ensure free and high-quality mandatory education for all children," he said. "Education is and should always be seen as a fundamental right. The state cannot run away from its responsibility."

Until that happens, the arithmetic remains stark. A school fee growing at 10 percent annually doubles every 7.2 years. A family currently paying ₹2.5 lakh per year will face a cumulative 12-year outlay closer to ₹55 to ₹60 lakh — before college, before coaching, and before the hidden costs that no brochure mentions.
